utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom, which is not as cold as the last few days. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I was informed that where the failure in the heating the last few days was fixed, that the next step to make is to fix the air conditioning, so that I hope that the temperature will go down. First of all, I'd like to know, Mr. Tieger, is there any response to a confidential motion which would cause us to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The Prosecution has reviewed both submissions. We're satisfied that there's more than sufficient information upon which the Court can base its determinations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then there's no need to go into private session. I might have some additional information for the Prosecution in respect of conflicting treaty obligations, or international obligations, but that would come later. Then, Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Customary in these circumstances in England for me to ask for permission to take my wig off, but I've already taken that step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I thought that you had taken the liberty already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it simply doesn't go with this clothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, just take care that you don't catch a cold sooner or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart [Continued]:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your evidence given on Wednesday, and for the reference, it's page 78, you said, when you were asked: "So that, for example, in relation to policing matters" -- please excuse me one moment, Your Honour. The headphones I've got on are not the same ones that are connected to the ... That's better. At page 78, it was, for everybody's reference, on Wednesday, you were asked by Mr. Tieger: "So that, for example, in relation to policing matters, you would most likely expect the instructions to come from the minister, minister of the interior or whatever the precise phraseology would be, that was responsible for policing." I think that yesterday, of course you're getting what I'm saying in translation, but when I used in English the phrase "minister of the interior," you seemed to be happy with that, Mr. Radic, as the label for that particular minister responsible for policing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having been asked that, you would most likely expect instructions to come from the minister, and you said: "Absolutely correct. That's what the case was before the war during the war, and it's still like that now. There is this subordination." And then, well, you were asked about instructions. But, Mr. Radic, you're not suggesting that the minister interfered with day-to-day policing matters in your region or your municipality, are you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- it is difficult to even assume that whenever anything happened he would not have been informed by the chief of the security services centre. He would have received a request by the minister to the effect of informing him as to what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm exploring with you, Mr. Radic, is this: That policing activity involves all sorts of on-the-ground actions which in some cases don't even get reported back to your local police station if they're just incidental matters in the course of a day, but that the minister - and this is correct, isn't it - the minister is only concerned in policing activities so far as larger policy issues or strategic issues or major problems are concerned?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of whether the minister deals only with strategic issues. That is the policy of the police. But the subordinates would receive orders from him and report back to him. I say that I merely assume that it could not have been otherwise because they did not have links with any other bodies, particularly not with the presidents of municipal assemblies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's be specific, Mr. Radic. Do you yourself have any personal knowledge of instructions or reports going backwards and forwards between the minister of the interior and the police in your region or your municipality, for that matter, in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of anything specific, but judging by the police activities, one could assume so. But I haven't seen these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you give an illustration of some specific instruction or report going backwards and forwards between the minister of the interior and the police in the region which you derive from some assumption or inference yourself?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us take, for instance, the dismissal -- the removal of people who have in any way tried to assist me in maintaining peace in the town of Banja Luka. At that point, they would be removed and replaced by others. From that, I infer that such an instruction had come from the ministry, because it was only the ministry that could have appointed or removed such people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a single example of such a removal or replacement?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the public security station, Mr. Vladimir Tutus, was replaced on account of that. Mr. Kutlija was replaced on account of that and was clearly informed as having been replaced for that reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your inference then is that his removal and replacement were on the instructions of the minister?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nobody else who could have removed him and appointed him immediately afterwards in Bijeljina, therefore, far from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've been asked quite a lot of questions, Mr. Radic, about what might or might not have been said to you, and that's what I want to explore, on the question of ethnic cleansing, deportation or some such other word or label in Banja Luka. On Wednesday this week, you were asked, and the transcript reference is page 31, you were asked by

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Did Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic" -- that's the order in which their names often get presented in this case: "Did Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic ever complain to you that Banja Luka had not been properly cleansed, that is, that there were still Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka?" And then you said: "The two of them never did, never directly." Then a little bit further on, foot of page 32, His Honour Judge Orie asked you whether they'd ever come one by one, just Mr. Karadzic, just Mr. Krajisnik, and complain to you, by whatever means, that Banja Luka had not been properly cleansed. You said you couldn't remember. And then His Honour asked about the meeting. And you said: "No, not at a meeting. No, there was no mention of that. The fact that Banja Luka would have to do the job or to give me instructions to do that. I must say that I would have refused quite certainly." Now, I want to try to clarify with you first, Mr. Radic. It seemed to be clear from your evidence yesterday that you never had any business meetings at which you and Mr. Krajisnik were present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that is not a correct presentation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wasn't it sit-down meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it also focused on the period prior to April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please -- Mr. Stewart, I do not remember, but perhaps I'm mistaken. Then please correct me. I think the question yesterday was about sit-down meetings and the limitation in time is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I put to the witness this morning, Your Honour, was -- well, I'm just looking to see. It seemed to be clear from your evidence yesterday that you never had any business meetings at which you and Mr. Krajisnik were present. Your Honour, that was based on the passage at page 81 of the transcript on Wednesday, when I asked the question: "Well, you've said a little bit earlier you had no meeting with him alone." And him was Mr. Krajisnik. "Just the two of you, because I asked you specifically. But it seems from the answer you've just given that the slightly wider meeting at which there was you, Mr. Krajisnik, and other, any other people, what you've said, just said, applies to that. You never had any specific meeting of that type, including Mr. Krajisnik; that's correct?" That was a question. The answer from Mr. Radic was: "I can even state quite certainly that even if we had a broader meeting with other people, it never had anything to do with any business decisions or anything like that. It was just -- happened to be a courteous exchange after some meeting and I state once again that I never had a meeting with Mr. Krajisnik, any contact with him, nor did he with me, because, quite simply, the jobs we did were different, so we didn't have any need to meet except at meetings of the Main Board, of course, but then I did not have a meeting with him. I was there with all the members of the Main Board." Well, I must say, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Business decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- seems to be absolutely supported and confirmed by that passage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it's now put to the witness in the right context, as far as time is concerned, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's the precisely right context, Your Honour. Page 80, Mr. Stewart says: "Let's give it a time frame now. In 1990, 1991, and 1992, so let's say from multi-party elections up to the start of the war, let's say, did you ever have any sit-down meeting with Mr. Krajisnik," et cetera. And that was the time frame upon which those questions were premised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To seek clarification, it doesn't -- you just have read the transcript of what the witness said, and could you please keep in mind that if there's any relevance of time, Mr. Stewart, that we will not miss it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I must say, Your Honour, that Mr. Tieger's objection was absolutely unfounded there, because apart from anything else, there are two points. First of all, the witness's answer appears to be perfectly general, but even if we assume that it's linked to the time frame I gave him, nobody could possibly be sensibly supposing that all this evidence in relation to the meetings with Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik could have taken place outside the time frame of 1991 and 1992. That would simply be absurd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the time frame posed by Mr. Stewart himself yesterday went up to April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question is whether the time frame further is the beginning of further questioning on something the witness had to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, Mr. Tieger should read what he's citing to the Court more carefully, because what I said at page 80 was: "Did you ever have -- let's give it a time frame now. In 1990, 1991, and 1992 so let's say from multi-party elections up to the start of the war, let's say." So that takes it from -- right through 1990, add an extra year 1991 and then up to the beginning of the war. So I'm prepared to take it to there but I will then, in order to clarify with this witness now:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you said yesterday -- I'm sorry -- on Wednesday -- you can state quite certainly that even if we had a broader meeting with other people it never had anything to do with any business decisions or anything like that, et cetera. And that's the passage that I read just now. Would that answer be different if we were talking about the period from April 1992 onwards? Tell me if the question is not clear.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is clear. I have already answered that question to the Prosecutor as well, yesterday, and I've said that up until the war, I knew of Mr. Krajisnik only through the National Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I had no direct contacts with him whatsoever. From the start of the war onwards, I also assert that I had no need for any such meetings, nor did I meet alone with Mr. Krajisnik. It was only at broader meetings that we possibly exchanged some words, but it was no special separate meeting between myself and Mr. Krajisnik, the two of us alone. That's what I've said yesterday and I repeat today. We would meet, but again, not the two of us alone, after the war, when I had a couple of contacts with Mr. Krajisnik. And that's what I've said yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Ms. Cmeric mentions to me that at line 15 on this page, page 9, line 15, where the transcript refers to no special separate meetings between myself and Mr. Krajisnik, the word "business" came -- in the witness's language, of course, but the word "business" came in there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's noted down and I take it it will be checked on the basis of the audio recording. Mr. Stewart, I think, as a matter of fact, it doesn't -- is of such influence that we couldn't continue. It's just for the transcript that it has been --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's just useful to make these observations as we go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I don't know there to be any doubt about this, Mr. Radic, so I want you to have a full opportunity to clear up any misunderstanding here. So your statement that: "Even if you and Mr. Krajisnik had a broader meeting with other people, it never had anything to do with business decisions or anything like that, which is your quoted answer, that applies to the whole time frame: 1990, 1991, 1992, and then, in fact, onwards from that date?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you agree, then, Mr. Radic, that having had no such meetings with Mr. Krajisnik, that any suggested meeting at which questions of the efficiency of ethnic cleansing or the efficiency or completeness of deportation or removal of non-Serbs from Banja Luka could not have taken place between you and Mr. Krajisnik, with or without other people being present?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- you've given a general answer, which logically covers this already, but nevertheless, so that there is no misunderstanding at all, I'm going to put it in the more limited, specific form. Did you ever receive any communication, in any form whatever, from Mr. Krajisnik, concerning ethnic cleansing, deportation, expulsion, removal of non-Serbs from anywhere to anywhere?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, the Chamber finds it necessary to inform you that the answer you've given about a meeting on which you testified yesterday in quite some detail, and where you now say that such a meeting could not have taken place, that it's difficult to reconcile these two answers, and that if one of the answers would not be the truth, that this could -- this could be understood as being a false testimony. Yesterday you answered some questions I put to you on a meeting with Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic, on which -- in which you said you were blamed for, and I'm not insisting on the precise wording, but you are blamed for not having expelled non-Serbs from Banja Luka, and as a result, that there were too many non-Serbs remaining in Banja Luka. And the answer you've just given seems to be difficult to reconcile with that. I'd just like to draw your attention to that and to make it clear to you that whenever you would not speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, that this might give rise to a suspicion of contempt. Please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed, Your Honour, to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any -- if you find any misunderstanding in -- misunderstanding on the part of the Chamber, then please address us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text that I have before me here, it said the end, three dots, then Karadzic. And then it said Kraj, K-r-j [as interpreted], that that was an error, that it wasn't Krajisnik, but Karadzic, and then and the question raised was why there were so many Muslims and Croats, and my answer was: That is true. The lawyer asked the quell quite clearly. He said: Did Mr. Krajisnik ever suggest to you that ethnic cleansing be conducted? And I said: No, never. And if you go back to what it says in the text, then it says: Kraj, K-r-a-j, three dots, then Karadzic, and then it says the error was that it said Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But -- well, of course, you were asked by Mr. Stewart about any meeting that would have taken place with Mr. Krajisnik, whether alone or with anyone else. So your answer this morning has not to be understood as a denial of what you said yesterday, that you had a meeting with Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In which Mr. Karadzic blamed you for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only him, but others too. Others blamed me too and criticised me for the fact that there were still Muslims and Croats, when all the other cities had been cleansed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at least in this one meeting where Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were present, that Mr. Karadzic expressed this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik didn't ask me that question. I said that he never asked me that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you whether Mr. Karadzic expressed that to you in a meeting you had together with Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Karadzic, as you testified yesterday, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday it was said that the K-r-a-j, three dots, was a mistake, that it was a mistake having mentioned Krajisnik at all. If you find the text, then you'll see the beginning of his name, K-r-a-j, three dots, and then it was said that it was a mistake, an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll read the relevant part of yesterday's transcript and see whether your answer today is in denial of your testimony of yesterday. One moment, please. If the matters could give me -- I have to find it, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What is it Your Honour is looking for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The questions I put to the witness yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it was at about, about page 47. There was a run of -- I think Your Honour is talking about the questions -- it was the hypothetical question that Your Honour put to the witness at page 47, I think. The whole run of the transcript, I think, begins around page 41, this particular issue, and then -- because Your Honour did ask some questions and make some comments from page 41 onwards. "Mr. Radic, you are explaining a lot to us now." That's page 41, line 12. "Why questions are put to you." And then we go on to ethnic cleansing and then there's a whole run of consideration of the issue until we get to page 47. Is that what Your Honour is seeking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Specific part. I'll put it to you at a later stage. I have difficulties in finding exactly what I'm trying to find. You may proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I don't know if it will be helpful, but I think Mr. Stewart mentioned page 47 at one point. It appears to me that he correctly identified the commencement of the questions the Court appears to be focused on, and it seems to conclude at page 48, the middle of page 48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's what Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's absolutely right. I -- yeah. It really goes down to about line 17 on page 48 and then we do go on to something else, linked, but a specific issue, which doesn't really carry the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I put it to you yesterday when we spoke about a meeting with Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic that you were blamed for not having expelled non-Serbs, and I asked you: "What did they then expect you to do with that?" That you would have to feed and to give medication to those present: "To leave them, that they would leave the area, that they would leave the territory so that there was no need to feed them any more. Is that what they suggested or what the one who spoke suggested?" And then your answer was: "They probably had meant that the same should be done as did the other side, that had expelled the Serbs and solved their problems that way, that is to say, the Croats and the Muslims." My next question was: "So then you are blamed for not having expelled non-Serbs, as Serbs were expelled from other territories with, as a result, that there were too many non-Serbs remaining in Banja Luka who had to be fed and -- is that a correct understanding of -- and had to be given medical care? Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?" And then you said: "You've understood it well." All these questions were put in the context of a meeting you had with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, in which Mr. Karadzic spoke the words, and therefore, I corrected myself when I said not they, but the one who spoke. Is the answer of this morning to be understood as a denial of such a meeting having taken place with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, or is this a misunderstanding? If ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that never with the two of them did I have a separate meeting at which that was discussed, a separate meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please clarify yourself. If it was not a separate meeting, what kind of a meeting then it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that there was some meeting, a broader kind of meeting, and that people would step to one side to discuss one topic, for example. So it wasn't with that particular purpose in mind, what we've just been discussing here, but we did step to one side, and I was blamed and criticised for the fact that there were so many Croats and Muslims in Banja Luka and in the executive organs of the Municipal Assembly as well, and in managerial posts and so on and so forth, when the case wasn't like that in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that it was not only the presence of non-Serbs in the governmental bodies, but also that you were blamed for not having expelled non-Serbs from the territory, which you had to feed and which you had to take, in medical terms, care of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because we asked them to send us the medicaments and food and everything else for the entire population. The Serbs were coming into us from Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas these other people weren't going anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And this was in Banja Luka in a meeting where Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a broader meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but where these two persons were present and where Mr. Karadzic was speaking; is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I just said that here, that Mr. Krajisnik never said that to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have to -- I now better understand that we have to make a distinction between separate meetings and meetings. But this is not a denial of what you testified yesterday; is that a proper understanding? Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if the witness could be asked to leave court for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's anything you'd like to raise in his absence. Mr. Radic, could you please follow for a moment ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour eventually got the witness to the position a few minutes ago where the witness denied that there was any contradiction between two pieces of evidence between which there is an absolute inevitable contradiction. There simply is. The problem, Your Honour, we submit, is this: That Your Honour has great authority sitting on the Bench, and Your Honour's brother Judges have great authority sitting on the Bench. We have had submissions before and we've had discussion, if I may respectfully put it that way, before about the ambit of questions from the Bench, and I made an objection a long time ago in relation to another witness altogether that was overruled, and Your Honour -- Your Honours said that it was only in the most exceptional circumstances there should be any objection to questions from the Bench and that those particular circumstances had not been exceptional, which left me struggling to think of circumstances which would be sufficiently exceptional. But the difficulty is that with the authority that the Bench has, our submission is that it is even more important for the Bench to take care in relation to leading questions than for counsel. And this witness we have seen; he has gone backwards and forwards. And if we now look at the evidence he's given this morning, and that's rather difficult for us to look at immediately, as a simply mechanical thing, but if we look at the evidence he's given this morning and we compare it carefully with the evidence he's given yesterday, and we compare it with what he said in the interviews, it's riddled with contradictions and it's riddled with acceptance by this witness of suggestions put to him by other people which he then subsequently withdraws. We are in a very dangerous area with a witness of this type when leading questions are put to him and he's invited to agree. But added to that, that Your Honour's warning, in effect, to this witness in relation to perjury, which, with respect, if Your Honour is giving the warning to the witness on the issue of perjury, we might have suggested to Your Honour it could be given even more explicitly than Your Honour gave it. So because if there is to be a warning at all, then it really needs to be in the absolutely -- in absolutely unequivocal terms and we suggest that that warning, if given as a warning, could be given more explicitly than it has been. But the difficulty with a warning like that is that it actually operates as a threat to a witness. I'm not suggesting, Your Honour, that of course that's Your Honour's intention. That would be quite improper. But that is the effect. Because when a witness comes along and gives evidence, and this may be an extreme case that we have here in court this morning, but it's a feature of evidence in criminal law, civil cases, for that matter, that witnesses do contradict themselves, that they do retract evidence, that they do -- sometimes they simply correct it. But they often do. Now, in practice, Your Honour, it's up to other people, perhaps, whether they launch prosecutions for perjury, in practice, prosecutions for perjury I think in any jurisdiction are extremely rare in relation to contradictions within the evidence that is given as opposed to evidence which is then provably false by comparison with external events. So realistically speaking, that doesn't happen, because, after all, that would be a tremendous disincentive to a witness to correct and retract his evidence as he goes along. So as a matter of policy, that would actually undermine the interest of justice, for witnesses to feel that inherent contradictions in the course of their evidence were going to expose them to such risks. That should not be the position. The position should be that a witness, as far as possible, ought to feel free to correct, retract, withdraw his evidence as he goes along in the case, and should be encouraged to do so, if at any point he feels that his earlier evidence was not correct. Because where one should end up with a witness is the witness saying: Well, I said this the other day. I might have said this the other day. You asked me this the other day. But this is what I am saying. And a reminder to the witness that he's given a solemn declaration, or in other jurisdictions he's on oath, may be appropriate, but what Your Honour has -- the position that Your Honour has put the witness in is that he's been told: Well, you answered a whole lot of questions to the Bench yesterday, and you've given some answers this morning under questioning by counsel, and the answers are inconsistent, which they plainly are, Your Honour. After all, that's what my job is, to some extent. They plainly are inconsistent. The answers are inconsistent. That inconsistency is exposing you to a risk. And then if I can put it this way, Your Honour: Have a hard rethink, Mr. Witness, about whether perhaps what you said yesterday in answer to questions from the Bench wasn't true. Your Honour, this is not intended that way, but it is in the end inordinate pressure on a witness to say: Well, yes. Actually, now you mention it, yes, what I did say to the Court yesterday was true. Your Honour, I was proposing anyway, of course, to explore and put to the witness aspects of what he said to the Court yesterday, because there is clearly a contradiction. But, Your Honour, I do invite the Trial Chamber to take note of the observations that I've just made and to proceed with great caution in relation to such matters. And please also, may I respectfully ask that when I, and my colleagues request speak for themselves, my colleagues on the other side of the case, but when I am cross-examining a witness and we are getting into the area of exposure of contradictions, that I might be allowed more latitude to continue with my cross-examination and to explore the matter on behalf of my client, not, of course, and I couldn't even presume to do that, because I can't -- the Bench has every right and duty and responsibility to then come in with whatever questions it feels appropriate at an appropriate stage. But I do particularly invite the Bench to allow in this essentially adversarial procedure, whatever the mixture of different systems, to have greater freedom to complete and -- proceed with and complete my cross-examination before we have the sort of exchanges and the sort of questioning that we've had over the last 20 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber will proceed with great caution. The Chamber deemed it necessary to give a warning and Rule 91(A) and briefly explain to the witness the reason why the Chamber at that moment wanted to give that warning. The witness then asked permission to address the Court, in which he explained that it was a matter of misunderstanding, and it was at that moment my duty to explore whether it was a misunderstanding or not. That's what I did. But the Chamber will proceed with great caution, as you asked the Chamber to do. You may proceed. Could we escort -- could you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, is it your position that you recall Dr. Karadzic complaining directly to you that there had not been insufficient steps taken to remove non-Serbs from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. Did you intend to say that there had not been insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't, Your Honour. Thank you. The double negative was unintended. But I'll do the whole question again. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, is it your position that you recall Dr. Karadzic complaining directly to you that there had been insufficient steps taken to remove non-Serbs from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These comments of his were not addressed to me only but to the entire leadership in the Assembly of the town of Banja Luka, especially those who were deputies and who were the ones who conveyed this message that more had to be done in order for the Muslims and Croats to leave to their areas, just as we've had Serbs arriving from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and from Croatia. So it was not addressed to me solely; it was a criticism levelled at the entire leadership. And once again, I emphasise: These were not formal meetings devoted to that purpose alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of your answer to that question, you said that: "These comments were addressed to the entire leadership in the Assembly of the town of Banja Luka." Let's be very clear, please, Mr. Radic. Which Assembly are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly of the town of Banja Luka and the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you talk of Dr. Karadzic addressing the entire leadership in the Assembly of the town of Banja Luka, was that a meeting of the Assembly of the town of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To the individuals from the Executive Board and to individuals from the legislative branch of government. One must know that some of the members of the Executive Board were also deputies and could also have discussions on this issue at Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I would not be able to tell you when the meeting was held. There were several meetings held on -- for several purposes, in Banja Luka, and again I repeat that these were not formal meetings convened for that particular purpose, for that particular matter that we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you have no idea, Mr. Radic, I want to press you a little bit. Let's take it in steps. Was it before or after the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the beginning of the war, not before the war. Before the war, we had a multi-party assembly that had its members in the Executive Board, and the government was a multi-ethnic one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. We had a multi-ethnic assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm told by Ms. Cmeric, and it would be quite a significant change, that that answer actually began: Before the beginning of the war and after the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, was your answer that it was before and after the beginning of the war? And we are now talking about the meetings where this issue was addressed. Did you say before and after, or after the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said that before the start of the war, there was no need for it, because both the executive and legislative branches of government were multi-ethnic. Therefore, before the war, there was no such thing. After the war, in the very beginning, both branches were still multi-ethnic, but it was only later when this practice was introduced in Bosnia-Herzegovina for the people, for the ethnicities to relocate. That's when this was the case. And that's what I said -- that's why I said not before the war, but after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that seems to be pretty clear, Your Honour, from the explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just remind us all, really, but you specifically, Mr. Radic: I'm asking you at the moment about a particular meeting that you have referred to. You're clear about that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that you're looking for a specific meeting, but I've told you that after the war, there were many meetings convened for different matters. There were some ceremonies as well, if you know what I mean by this. If there was some sort of a purpose to celebrate something, then you would have the leadership of Banja Luka convened, and it was also at that time that this matter would be raised, because it was quite obvious that the numbers of the Croat and Muslim populations present in Banja Luka were much higher than elsewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I don't know how the phrase gets translated into Serbian, but in English, we are going round the houses here with you. So please, I'm not looking for a specific meeting. Your evidence has been of a specific meeting, and therefore, I am asking you questions about that meeting. So let's go back to where we were. I am -- this particular meeting that you referred to, at which Dr. Karadzic addressed the leadership in Banja Luka, leadership of the Assembly, and so on, you said it took place after the beginning of the war, and you explained why. Did it take place, as far as you recall, during the period when Banja Luka, the Krajina, was cut off from south-eastern Bosnia, certainly, i.e., that is, between the beginning of the war and the 26th of June when the corridor was opened?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's take it from the end. There wasn't a single meeting. That's what I keep repeating. There was not just one meeting, nor was it a meeting with the entire leadership. Rather, there were several contacts through which we received information about the dissatisfaction with our actions in this particular matter. Of course, that all this took place after the war, rather, after the opening up of the corridor. Therefore, from April up until 1994, 1995. But I wasn't referring to a single meeting with the entire municipal leadership present, where Mr. Karadzic assigned certain tasks to us. Mr. Karadzic was exposed to the pressure of those who were saying that this had not been done in Banja Luka, whereas they had in their respective parts done everything. That's why we still had mosques left standing and that's why we still had Muslims and Croats living there, because we did not adhere to some unwritten rules valid in the rest of Republika Srpska. So I was not referring to a single meeting where we were given this task. And please do not insist on a single meeting, because it was not just that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say it wasn't just that one, Mr. Radic, was that meeting that you referred to a few minutes ago one of a number of meetings?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say, for instance, festivities, that could be the celebration of the patron saint of Banja Luka, where the president of the Republic would come. There would be a festivity, following which he would say that we had not done what others had. The other occasion could be at Pale, when you would have deputies from Banja Luka present there, and they would happen to say that we had not done in our town what others have done in Republika Srpska. Therefore, it wasn't just one meeting, nor was there this particular one meeting where it had been stated that we should do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic. How many times did Dr. Karadzic come to Banja Luka after the beginning of the war up to the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am really unable to answer the question of how many times he arrived there. Sometimes he would not go to Banja Luka at all, because he had other obligations and would go about fulfilling them. It is very difficult for me to say how many times he was in that part that we call Krajina and how many times he visited Banja Luka. I don't remember. But it was on quite a few occasions that he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you clap eyes on Dr. Karadzic between the beginning of the war and the end of 1992 in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I knew the answer to that question, I would be able to tell you how many times he visited there. I really do not recall how many times I saw him, how many times and what the occasions were, and so on. There were, for instance, there was the promotion inauguration of recruits in the Army of Republika Srpska, the celebration of the patron saint of Banja Luka, then the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, I told you that we would hold the National Assembly in different towns, or when he would pass through Banja Luka and just inform us that he was there. But he was on his way and went on. Now, if I were able to tell you how many times I saw him, I would be able to tell you how many times he came. That is, however, difficult for me. He did tour Republika Srpska as president of Republika Srpska. How many times, I cannot say, and I would not like to give an incorrect number and then be told by His Honour that I did not state a correct number of visits by Mr. Karadzic. But there were quite a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope it's entirely for His Honour what directions he gives to you, Mr. Radic, but I believe that His Honour might say to you that doing your honest best to remember or to give the answers to these questions and to remember such things as how many times somebody came is not going to cause you any problems or dangers or risks. If you are doing your honest best to produce such information as accurately or as approximately as you can remember, I don't believe there will be a difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope that's a fair summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic. Mr. Radic, a question is put to you as to the number of meetings. If you say: Well, it's my recollection there were approximately 25 or 50 or 3 or 8, please tell us, if you can; if you cannot, then of course you can't answer that question. But since you said there were quite a few, if you could be more precise, even if you'd be not sure about the exact number, please give that answer. If you can't, then you can't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would perhaps be close to the number of 20 meetings, possibly 20 meetings, on different occasions, because when we had the patriarch of the Orthodox Church coming, and then there were other occasions as well, not only when there were Assembly sessions and then he had some business matters to deal with me. Therefore, let's say about 20 times that he visited or passed through Banja Luka and informed us that he was there during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have I got my logic right, Mr. Radic? It seemed to follow from an answer you gave earlier that Mr. Karadzic did not come and would not have come to Banja Luka during that period without your seeing him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were occasions when he did arrive without me seeing him. He would merely spend a night there and then continue onwards. And actually, as a rule, I never knew where he was going to spend the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radic, may I simply make it clear: This isn't a question, but just so that it can help us to proceed. You see, you're the witness giving evidence, and when you give an answer and then I proceed to ask you questions on the footing or on the basis of the answer that you've just given, that's -- I have to do that, Mr. Radic. So when you tell me and tell the Tribunal, as you did a few minutes ago, that if you knew how many times you'd clapped eyes on Dr. Karadzic during that period, you would know how many times Dr. Karadzic had been in Banja Luka, I, in my simple way, draw the inference that when Dr. Karadzic came to Banja Luka, you must have seen him. Do you follow? There is a question at the end. Do you understand why it is that I put questions to you in that form? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do understand you, and I am answering your questions to His Honours, and I said that I've seen him for some 20 times perhaps. And now when you ask me were there occasions that he would visit without you seeing him. Well, there were. I would hear of his arrival, especially towards the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Radic, of course I'm primarily concerned, let's make it clear, with occasions on which you, at least as a minimum saw Dr. Karadzic. Leave aside when he passed through without you having any dealings with him at all. Do your best, Mr. Radic. Between the beginning of the war and the end of 1992, how many times do you say that you saw, with your eyes, Dr. Karadzic in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said that. Around 20, perhaps 25 times at most. That's what I've said. I suppose it was some 20 times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And same question, but applied to Mr. Krajisnik. How many times did you clap eyes on Mr. Krajisnik in Banja Luka between the beginning of the war and the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would mostly see him during the sessions of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska in Banja Luka, when these sessions were in Banja Luka. That's when I was invited to attend the Assembly as a host, as president of the Municipal Assembly. Otherwise, as I said, I did not meet with Mr. Krajisnik alone on other occasions. So these would be the kind of occasions that I would see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So doing your best, Mr. Radic, what was the answer to my question: How many times did you clap eyes on Mr. Krajisnik in Banja Luka between the beginning of the war and the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As many times as the number of sessions held there. There could have been maybe three or four sessions held in Banja Luka. Otherwise, they would hold them in Prijedor, Bijeljina, I believe also in Brcko, at Pale, and Trebinje, and so on. Therefore, some three to four times. But I cannot tell you the exact number. That's when the National Assembly was convened in Banja Luka, and Mr. Krajisnik would be there. In addition to that, he might have been invited to some of the festivities there, but this was very rarely. Mr. Krajisnik spent most of his time at Pale and perhaps in the eastern part. But in the -- this western part, particularly in Banja Luka, I don't believe that he was there more often than for the times when the National Assembly met in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is this right, then, Mr. Radic. It may seem obvious, but I just want to get it clear: That if we check, because there are such records, then if we check to see how many sessions of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska, previously known as Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but how many sessions of that assembly were held in Banja Luka from the public records, that's going to give me the answer to the question I just asked you: How many times was Mr. Krajisnik in Banja Luka. That would tell us, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would tell you, but I cannot recall how many sessions the Assembly had in Banja Luka. If there were five of them, then the occasions were five. But I don't believe that there were more than four sessions held there, because the sessions were also held in other towns. And of course, most often, it was convened at Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I don't need to trouble you on anything which is easily checkable from obtainable records. We don't need to worry about that. I just want to make it clear, then: You said he might have been invited to some of the festivities there, but this was very rarely. So can we take it that if he was, which you apparently don't know, those were certainly not visits on which any business discussions took place in which you and Mr. Krajisnik were participants?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on any of the occasions -- we are at the moment dealing with that period, from the beginning of the war through to the end of 1992. But on any of those occasions that Mr. Krajisnik, you say, came to Banja Luka for Assembly sessions, Assembly of Republika Srpska, do you say that there were any business discussions at which you and Mr. Krajisnik were present outside the Assembly meetings themselves?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, if I put it to you that there were two Assembly sessions of Assembly of Republika Srpska in 1992, after the beginning of the war, held in Banja Luka, the first on the 12th of May, 1992 - and we see that very clearly, actually, from documentation that's in court for the course of your evidence - the first on 12th of May, 1992, and the second spread over two days, 11th and 12th of August, 1992, does that at least match what you can remember?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't understood you. What is it that I'm supposed to remember?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll put it -- that perhaps wasn't crystal clear, Mr. Radic. I'll put it again. I'm putting to you that -- first of all, before we get to the actual question. I'm putting it to you that there were two sessions of the Assembly of Republika Srpska held in Banja Luka in 1992, after the beginning of the war. One was on the 12th of May, 1992, and the next one was over two days, on the 11th and 12th of August, 1992. I'm asking you whether you remember anything to contradict what I've just said, that there were just those two meetings of the Republika Srpska Assembly during that period, up to the end of 1992, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the end of 1992, not up until the end of the war. Quite possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I specifically said up until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I've said four to five. You say two. But that's until the end of 1992. It is possible that there were only two sessions until the end of 1992, but to tell you the truth, what the -- what was discussed at these sessions, that's something I cannot remember. But it is quite possible that there were these two sessions there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If -- well, if there were -- Mr. Radic, take it from me. There were at least meetings of the Assembly of Republika Srpska in Banja Luka on those dates. That's not going to be an issue in this case. First of all, do you now, having been given those dates, can you say that you were at both of those sessions, in May and August 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will again use the term "possibly," but as a guest. I was not a deputy. I would be invited as a guest to listen at the debates of the National Assembly. Most frequently, Mr. Stewart, since I had other town-related businesses to attend, I would usually leave the Assembly after -- at the interval, because I did not have the right of addressing them, just of listening to them. So it is possible that I was there, but as a guest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's extremely close to the time when we customarily have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually have a break, yes. Could you give us any indication on the question which --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to give consistent answers, Your Honour. I'm -- of course, I -- in the light of the way things have gone, of course I'm going to be longer. What I do know, Your Honour, is that I do have a little bit of material which Mr. Krajisnik brought with him first thing this morning. So I don't know what that includes. But, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You sometimes invite persons to give an approximate number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I'm going to do that. No. I'm going to say that I -- I am confident that I won't go beyond the next break, Your Honour. I'm not so confident about saying more than that, not having reviewed this particular material. But I think it unlikely that I would need to go the whole of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, your confidence of yesterday has been shaken a bit already, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not entirely within my control, Your Honour, as Your Honour I know accepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wanted to say something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break until 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think it's why I didn't give a guarantee, Your Honour. I was that careful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a small point on the transcript which could conveniently be dealt with while the witness is coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm trying to read it and stay near enough to a microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's at page 22, line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the answer, which I tried to correct, but apparently I still got it wrong again. "After the beginning of the war, not before the war" - that's all right, that sentence, apparently - and then the next sentence: "Before the war" and then it should include "and after the beginning of the war, we had a multi-party assembly." So that's where the reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what he explained later, during a short period of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- created some slight confusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So specific attention will be paid to that portion of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you talked about, almost in passing, in a sense, but you mentioned that deputies who were present in Banja Luka for Assembly meetings of the Republika Srpska Assembly said something to you about the position in Banja Luka relating to the presence of non-Serbs. That's right, is it, that deputies of the Republika Srpska Assembly broached that topic with you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the deputies of Republika Srpska, I don't remember whether there were five or six of them from Banja Luka in the National Assembly itself. They just conveyed the opinion that in Banja Luka there were far greater number of non-Serbs than there were Serbs in other municipalities. Of course, they never conveyed any directives that this should be cleansed, but it was a criticism to us in the authorities in Banja Luka, because of that fact. And that was true. There were more Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka than there were Serbs in the municipalities where they were the majority population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't -- or you wouldn't have accepted it as a valid criticism; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the truth. It was true that we had more Muslims and Croats in our town than there were Serbs, for example, in Sarajevo, Bihac, which had been completely cleansed and still is today, and so on and so forth. So that was true. But we couldn't reconcile ourselves to doing the same thing they had done, that is to say, to expel part of the population, people like that were coming in to Banja Luka and telling us what had happened to them in those towns that they were expelled from. Quite simply, Banja Luka could not act in similar fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's right that you -- you say it was a fact, it was the truth, if you compare the numbers. But what I put to you is correct, isn't it, that you wouldn't have accepted that as a valid criticism of any actions or inactions on your part?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How we took this criticism is borne out by the fact that at the end of the war in that exodus afterwards was the largest exodus of citizens from Banja Luka that took place, according to Cornelio Sommaruga's observation and we did not accept this as an order having to do that forcibly. From our conduct and behaviour you can see how we understood this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the deputies bring any pressure on you in connection with this? I'm talking about those five deputies that you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't bring pressure to bear. But they just told us of this stance of theirs. And as I say, there were people working in the municipality to whom the deputies conveyed this and, for example, there was a misunderstanding that I myself had with the president of the Executive Board, insisting that his vice-president, Antun Ruzic, who was a Croat himself, should remain in that post because he wasn't able to get another job in Banja Luka. He was ill himself and he had some children that he had to bring up. And unfortunately, he died after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to explore with you, Mr. Radic, an answer which you gave a little while ago before the break. You had said that Mr. Krajisnik might have come to Banja Luka at the time of - just wait until I've given the question, Mr. Radic - that he might have come to Banja Luka at the time of festivities, and you didn't know, but he might have done, and I asked you, and you said: Well, if he did, then there weren't any business meetings. And I was -- business meetings, I was really picking up a phrase from your evidence which you've talked about business. So there weren't any business meetings. Now, I want to be crystal clear from you, please, Mr. Radic. If, and it's an if, if Mr. Krajisnik did come to Banja Luka on any other occasion from the beginning of the war until the end of 1992, than the Assembly meetings of Republika Srpska, you didn't have any sort of political discussion meeting with Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Krajisnik and others, did you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two questions there in one. First, whether I remember if Mr. Krajisnik came, and then if he did come, did I have a meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, let's be clear. Actually --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So do you want me to answer the second question first?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, we all fall into that trap sometimes, but actually there aren't two questions. It's based on a hypothesis. You said you weren't sure whether -- it might become. So the question is a single question. After all, if he didn't come then for heaven's sake there's no question because you can't have had a meeting with him if he didn't come. But if he did come, it's the single question whether you had any sort of political discussion, meeting, with Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Krajisnik and others on those occasions.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I said that Mr. Krajisnik did come when there were National Assembly meetings of Republika Srpska. And I state again that after those sessions there were no political talks with Mr. Krajisnik as the English would say, face to face. I didn't have any face to face meetings with him. Does that satisfy you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It will have to, up to a point, Mr. Radic. You're anticipating a further question. I think I'm going to scrap the one I asked you before. You've brought us back to the occasions on which he did come to Banja Luka for Assembly meetings. So I'm going to operate on your territory here, Mr. Radic, and ask you about that. When he did come to Banja Luka then for Assembly meetings of Republika Srpska, you say there were no political talks with Mr. Krajisnik, as the English would say, and we do, face to face. You didn't have any face-to-face meetings with him. Can I be clear that apart from anything you heard Mr. Krajisnik say to the Assembly, that you participated in no other discussions on any political issues at all at which Mr. Krajisnik and you were both present?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean at the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I mean apart from the actual Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik and I were members of the Main Board of the SDS, but that, once again, wasn't face-to-face meetings; it was a group of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just leave aside the Main Board for the moment, then, Mr. Radic. We are talking about the occasions on which Mr. Krajisnik -- well, all right. Let's clarify this. We're talking about the occasions on which Mr. Krajisnik came to Banja Luka for Assembly meetings of Republika Srpska. Now, you're saying, are you, that on those occasions - and we've only identified two, in fact - on those occasions, you're saying there might have also been a Main Board meeting? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I wasn't clear on whether you were asking me whether I talked to Mr. Krajisnik after the Assembly session or on some other occasion. And I said to you that after the Assembly, I did not have a chance of having any kind of discussion with Mr. Krajisnik. And yes, I was at the Main Board with him, but that is not an Assembly meeting. So are we talking about meetings after the Assembly or perhaps after any kind of meeting whatsoever? Because there were different types of meetings, not only the National Assembly, not only meetings of the Main Board. There was, for example, the Holy Synod Assembly session meeting, with the patriarch, Mr. Pavle, arrived. So I can only assume that at one of those two meetings Mr. Krajisnik was probably present. I assume, I don't claim, because I can't actually remember whether he was in Banja Luka when the Holy Synod had its meeting. But I didn't have any talks with him on that occasion either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's try -- I'm going to put a --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, it says here "the Holy Sinard." It's not "Sinard". It's Synod, S-y-n-o-d.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected, Mr. Radic. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, and that's how I was spelling it in my own head as we were hearing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to put a proposition to you, Mr. Radic, and I just want you please, as I'm sure you always do, I want you to listen very carefully and tell me whether you agree with the proposition. The proposition is this: That on the occasions when Mr. Krajisnik came to Banja Luka, according to your evidence, for Assembly meetings of Republika Srpska from April to December 1992, there were no political meetings or discussions in which you and he were both -- or at which you and he were both present, apart from the Assembly sessions themselves? Now, is the proposition clear?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I cannot remember that ever afterwards, after the meetings of the National Assembly, that there were any gatherings at which anything like that was reviewed. If there is something to bear that out, please remind me of it. But as I say, I cannot remember that there were any political gatherings or meetings at all which was -- which did not have to do with the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "afterwards," because you've used that phrase, can we take it the same applies to before, during, or after the Assembly meetings on those occasions when the Assembly took place in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were, since I was not a deputy myself, I was not able to attend meetings of that kind. Before the Assembly, of course, people would be convened to the deputies to agree and coordinate their views with the president of the Assembly, but I had nothing to look for there because I wasn't a deputy myself. Now, during the Assembly meeting itself, there were no interruptions to discuss any separate issues, and after the Assembly sessions, if there was an analysis of any kind then it was an analysis of the Assembly, to which I, as a guest, had nothing to do there. I was a guest, in the capacity of guest, not as a member of parliament on a footing of equality with everybody else, the popular assembly, Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You agree, Mr. Radic, that on occasions of political meetings, where there are a lot of people there, this is standard, isn't it, and nothing special, perhaps, to where you were living and working, there were people milling around, there are formal meetings, there are informal meetings, there are people running into each other in the corridor, there are people perhaps having a cup of coffee or in the bar or whatever. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. That's politics. There are lots and lots of those types of discussions going on, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd exclude politics when I'm having a cup of coffee. Yes, we did have a cup of coffee, and I can't say that we held political discussions over coffee. There would be chatting afterwards, but it wouldn't be a political discussion. Of course, there were political meetings, including the meetings that were mentioned yesterday and the day before by the Prosecutor, for instance. But after that, we would go our own ways, go our separate ways, very quickly after that. There were no further political discussions. And let me say straight away that, as far as Mr. Krajisnik is concerned, I had very few contacts with him, very little contact with him. If you insist upon this matter, I would like somebody to refresh my memory and remind me when it was that I could have had a meeting with him, because quite simply, as I say, his job was one, mine was another. When he came to the Assembly meetings at Banja Luka, I myself was a guest. When we were at the Main Board, I would go back quickly, not have to spend the night there, because it's a long way from Pale to Banja Luka. You have to go a roundabout way, a circuitous route. So I didn't have occasion to talk to Mr. Krajisnik at all, and he was there too as a member, as I was myself. Perhaps in terms of hierarchy, he was somewhat higher up, but he wasn't the person that I would talk to after Main Board meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was between April and December 1992, there was simply no occasion on which Mr. Krajisnik was present, together with you and others, at which any questions of ethnic cleansing, deportation, expulsion, removal of non-Serbs from Banja Luka, could have taken place; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And beyond the end of 1992, does what I've just put to you and what you've just agreed with apply also to the whole of 1993?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it right that you have no specific recollection of any occasion on which Dr. Karadzic raised with you or in your presence, apart from Assembly sessions, any questions of ethnic cleansing, deportation, expulsion, removal of non-Serbs from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that it was his criticism mostly of what we had not done and what the others had done, and this could have been interpreted, and we interpreted it as a criticism, directed at the leadership of the town of Banja Luka, which had failed to do what the other towns had done, not only in Republika Srpska but even more so in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was that criticism expressed -- well, was that criticism expressed to you by Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he expressed this criticism to me and to the people who had greater connections with Pale, such as the deputies. When they go there, he would say: Gentlemen, you didn't -- haven't done what the other municipalities have done, for example so that would reach us down below. Of course, we had different views on the matter. The result was that Banja Luka was the last from which people left. And as I say, most of the people left in 1995, after the month of August. And similarly, it is also true and a fact that in Banja Luka there is not a single mass grave. However much you may search for any. I said I would be willing to dig myself if anybody found a mass grave anywhere. Looting and killings did occur, but there's not a single mass grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Karadzic ever express that criticism to you on any occasion when you and he were both physically present?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he ever express that criticism to you in a telephone conversation between you and him?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said he didn't, neither in a telephone conversation or in writing. He only sent one letter to me, corresponded with me once in writing, to inform me that the commission would re-examine some of my stands, positions. When I had an 11-member commission examining me on some of my positions, that is the only occasion that he used his right as president vis-a-vis me, the president of the Municipal Assembly. And I'm sure you have that document yourself. The establishment of a commission to assert the exactness of the allegations I had made in interviews given to various newspapers, journals, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you were asked yesterday some questions by His Honour Judge Orie, and we've been over some of this ground already this morning, but I'm afraid we are going to have to go over some of it again to get everything as clear as we possibly can. His Honour asked you, in relation to the interview that you'd -- that had been conducted in July 1991, at which -- sorry, 2001. I beg your pardon. July 2001 -- that if Ms. Korner - perhaps you remember Ms. Korner - but if Ms. Korner had asked you whether, during this meeting or such meetings - and that was a reference to supposed meetings with Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik - you had been blamed for there being too many remaining non-Serbs in Banja Luka, whether you would have been less hesitant to say: Yes, that's what they blamed me for. And then you referred to criticisms and so on. And then a little bit later on - it's page 48 of the transcript - His Honour said: "So then you are blamed for not having expelled non-Serbs, as Serbs were expelled from other territories, with, as a result, that there were too many non-Serbs remaining in Banja Luka who had to be fed, and is that a correct understanding of, and had to be given medical care? Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?" And you said: "You've understood it well." And His Honour put to you: "And that's what was said in meetings you had with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?" And you said: "Along those lines. Those were the suggestions made mostly. Nobody ever mentioned the methods of ethnic cleansing at all," and so on. Now, when His Honour put to you: "And that's what was said in meetings you had with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik" and you said "along those lines."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just, Mr. Stewart, interrupt you for one second. If you would look at the line starting my question with the words "and that's." And if you would then look at the sixth word, in connection with the fifth word, I am not quite sure that not the word "a" should be added, and perhaps the "s" stricken out from that sixth word. I'm not sure, but I'd like to check as a matter of fact on the audiotape what I exactly said. I'm just saying this to you at this moment in order to avoid whatever discussion later on I had -- of course, you can continue on the basis of this, but I just want to tell it to you now and not say: Well, if you had that in your mind, you should have told me at the time. I think I used the wording such that you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's very helpful and I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we should --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- our next breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I very much appreciate the slightly coded and understandable way in which Your Honour has put the point to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour and I are being asked to speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But I -- we -- so we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise also on behalf of Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I appreciate that. The -- Your Honour, it's -- I'm nearly at the end. It's such an important point, Your Honour, that I really think we should be clear before I proceed. It's a nuisance, I know, but it is a very important area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd have any other issue at this moment to deal with, we could do that. Otherwise, if we have a break now, we would be -- we might not -- we might have too long a period until the -- until the next -- too long a period for ending at a quarter to 2.00. So if you would have another subject, and I'll certainly try to do my utmost best to see whether we can clarify the issue I just raised during the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
