utterances.text: I don't know whether it's good news or bad news, Your Honour, but I don't have other points. So that indicates that my cross-examination shouldn't be very much longer, but it does present the immediate practical question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Stewart, I think we should have a break at this moment, and whether we could deal with the matter in 20 minutes or not is still to be seen. I'll see whether it will be possible to have an excerpt of the audio of that very moment to see whether we can -- I'm not sure. I'm simply saying this. I'm not sure. But I just thought that if it would be the case, then it could have some consequences which I'd rather avoid to occur. We'll have a break for at least 20 minutes, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would be wisest to have a break until a quarter past 12.00. We adjourn until a quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I checked during the break the transcript. The reason why I did this, because I had in the back of my mind that I not only used the plural, but also the singular. As a matter of fact, I did that, but one page prior to that, where I said meeting or meetings, this meeting or meetings. And I wasn't sure that it was where I said it. I checked it, and the transcript is correct in every respect. So that could be the basis for further questions. Before we do so, however, I'd like to ask a few questions to the Prosecution, but in private session. It will not take very long, I take it, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Radic, just to refresh our memories here on the immediate past, I'm talking about at page 47 of yesterday's transcript at -- I'm sorry. Page 48 we'd got on to. I'll just recap. His Honour Judge Orie said: "So then you were blamed for not having expelled non-Serbs, as Serbs were expelled from other territories, with, as a result, that there were too many non-Serbs remaining in Banja Luka who had to be fed and - is that a correct understanding of - and had to be given medical care. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?" And then you said: "You've understood it well." And Judge Orie said: "And that's what was said in meetings you had with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?" And then you said: "Along those lines. Those were the suggestions made mostly." And then, so, Mr. Radic, as an observation first, before I then get to the question: It appears that -- well, I'll put it in the form of a question. It appears that you were accepting what was implicit in His Honour's question, that discussions of these matters had taken place in meetings that you had had with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. So, first of all, do you agree that what I have just quoted to you from the transcript certainly appears to contain your acceptance of that implicit element of His Honour's question, that there were such meetings of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik at which there were such discussions?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that yesterday. However, I also said that such criticisms were not levelled at me by Mr. Krajisnik but by Mr. Karadzic. And that was written down, although I don't have it here on the screen. That's what I said. I said that this was not done by Mr. Krajisnik but by Mr. Karadzic. Later on, I also said that Mr. Krajisnik did not discuss this topic with me, be it individually with me, the two of us alone, or at meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you, in effect, accepted what His Honour was saying, that that was what was said in meetings you had with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, and you said "along those lines," that was as to the content, but you didn't dispute or comment or protest in any way at the assumption there had been such meetings, did you understand His Honour's question to relate only to meetings of the Assembly of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not formal meetings convened for that particular topic we've been discussing here. These were meetings convened after the Assembly session for some other purposes. And once again, I emphasise that I was not given any sort of an order to ensure that non-Serb populations left the area. I was simply criticised for having many more Croats and Muslims in Banja Luka than Serbs in the other areas. And this was written down. But I've also said that this was not something that Krajisnik said. And if you look back at what was said, it can't be seen here, you'll see that that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, the -- I have been reading transcript of your interview in July 2001, transcripts of your evidence that you've been giving in this trial in the course of this week, and I have been listening and/or reading to -- or listening to and/or reading what you've been saying this morning about all this. And I apologise that this isn't a question. This is simply a statement. At the moment, Mr. Radic, I am having great difficulty in reconciling your answers, which is why I'm exploring it. Mr. Radic, according to the evidence which you have given this morning, there were no such meetings that you had with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik at which this question of non-Serbs being expelled or removed from Banja Luka was discussed. That's correct, isn't it? That's been your evidence this morning.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no, so to speak, explicit statements to the effect that's what the case is, ethnic cleansing has to be carried out. We were being criticised for the fact that there were more Croats and Muslims in our municipality than there were elsewhere, in other areas. I've been saying this several times now. These were not statements concerning ethnic cleansing. These were just passing references by Mr. Karadzic, and I said that there was not a single occasion when Mr. Krajisnik addressed me on this topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, it goes further, doesn't it? You have been saying this morning, and I'm just inviting you to make it as clear as can be made, that there was not a single occasion on which the question of ethnic cleansing, expulsion, removal of non-Serbs from Banja Luka was discussed when you and Mr. Krajisnik were both present, if we leave aside Assembly sessions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've tried to give Mr. Stewart as much latitude as possible, but I think it's clear now that that question has been asked and answered, more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, many questions have been asked and answered more than once, but -- well, I'll go a small way with the witness present, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll allow you to put this question to the witness. I wouldn't fully disagree with what you said in response to that. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Radic, I'll put -- Mr. Stewart is putting to you that this morning, at various moments, you said: Well, there could not have been such meetings or such occasions where we could have discussed this matter. And he says that this is difficult to reconcile with what you told us yesterday and what was just put to you. That's, I think, the question Mr. Stewart is putting to you. He said: How could you say that such meetings could not have taken place, and at the same time, you told us about such a meeting yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kept saying here that a formal meeting dedicated to what was now discussed by Mr. Stewart never took place, that this was always on the occasion of something else taking place, whether an Assembly session or something else. It was on that occasion that I would be criticised for the large numbers of the Muslims and the Croats. Now, here you keep insisting on this one meeting being held for that, and I keep saying that there was no such one meeting dedicated to this particular issue. And specifically, Mr. Krajisnik never told me, not even at a broader meeting, involving more persons, anything about ethnic cleansing. And I don't know how many times I ought to repeat this in order to really say what I am supposed to be saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All you're supposed to be saying, Mr. Radic, is the truth, as best you can remember it. That's absolutely basic. So let's proceed on that footing. Also, Mr. Radic, I'm going to have to invite you, please, not to concern yourself with how many times you might have previously answered a particular question. That is a matter for the Trial Chamber to concern themselves with and to give directions on, and it's a matter on which we counsel have responsibilities. It is not your problem. Please, when you're asked a question, even if you think you've been asked it a hundred times, if you're asked the question, please answer it. Mr. Radic, was there ever an occasion on which you and Mr. Krajisnik were both present when Dr. Karadzic made any sort of criticism in relation to ethnic cleansing, expulsion, removal, deportation, presence of numbers of non-Serbs in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that there was. But the last part you mentioned, that was what was mentioned, the greater numbers of Muslims and Croats. But there was no mention of ethnic cleansing. But it is possible that there was this issue discussed. That's why I insisted on that error where the names of Krajisnik and Karadzic were put together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, and just to remind you: His Honour's questions yesterday, in effect, accommodated your objection to the phrase "ethnic cleansing," and so the gist of His Honour's questions were: Well, if we take away ethnic cleansing and we talk in terms of expulsion, then would your evidence be different, in effect, or would you accept such-and-such a position. And that's how it proceeded. So -- and the answer you've just given, you said, and you've given evidence to that effect, that the numbers of non-Serbs remaining in Banja Luka came up in some discussions. But let's take it in stages. Was there ever an occasion on which you and Mr. Krajisnik were both present when Dr. Karadzic made any sort of criticism in relation to ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether Mr. Krajisnik was there or not, I cannot claim with certainty. I say it is possible. But I do know that it was Mr. Karadzic who criticised me. Now, whether Mr. Krajisnik was there, I cannot confirm. And I've been saying this from the very beginning. Why put Krajisnik and Karadzic together at all costs, when Mr. Krajisnik never expressed this criticism, be it individually or in a meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, it's not for you to put questions to why certain persons are united in one question. If you would, however, like to know, it would be on the basis of your statement. Now, the issue is: You have told us yesterday that you are not happy with the ethnic cleansing expression, that that was not the terms that were used. You also told us that in meetings with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, the remaining numbers of non-Serbs in Banja Luka was put to you and that you were blamed for not having done the same as was done in other municipalities. You made clear to us that it was Mr. Karadzic who expressed those words. And you also testified that it was during meetings with -- or at least a meeting with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik being present. Is this correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When talking about Mr. Karadzic, the answer is yes. As for Mr. Krajisnik, it is possible that he was there, because the nature of the meetings was such that we were all there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday you told us that, when I specifically asked you whether this was said in meetings with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, you, as you did this morning, you confirmed that that was the case. I think you also explained to us that this was a meeting which was not a formal meeting of the Assembly, but that it was just in the margin of such meetings. Where you now say that it was possible that Mr. Krajisnik was present, when you said yesterday this was said at meetings where Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic were present although Mr. Karadzic expressed those words. Do we have to understand you -- answer of today to say that yesterday, when you said it was in meetings with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik that that was not a correct answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not saying that Mr. Krajisnik was not there with Mr. Karadzic. But it does not mean that he took part in it all. It was Mr. Karadzic who told me what I told you. And it wasn't Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik was not expressing those words, he was not -- he did not take part in it, but was he present, at least during one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was present, as I say, but he did not take part in the conversation, nor did he say anything on that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber considers the subject sufficiently dealt with at this moment. So you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What subject, Your Honour, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The subject of the presence of Mr. Krajisnik at an occasion where Mr. Karadzic expressed words on the issue of too many non-Serbs remaining in the Banja Luka area. And I think that this is what the issue is really about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask for the witness to leave court, please, before I make my next submission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My submission is very simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is absolutely the wrong approach. This is an absolutely unfair approach to adopt. We have been to-ing and fro-ing with this witness with him chopping and changing his answers. The Trial Chamber has exercised its prerogative to ask extremely leading questions, and the witness has gone backwards and forwards and at the point where Your Honour has led the witness back to the position in which the Prosecution largely want him to be, the Trial Chamber is then saying the subject is closed. In the middle of my cross-examination, the Trial Chamber intervenes, undermines the answers which I have obtained out of the witness, and the contradictions I've obtained out of the witness, leads him back to this point and then says that's the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It's not the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The end of the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The contradiction in the answer is still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, let's not discuss the matter any further, Mr. Stewart. The Chamber is not unaware that this witness testified that he had a meeting with Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic where Mr. Karadzic spoke about certain subjects. The Chamber is also not unaware that the witness also testified that such meetings could not have taken place at the same time, that such meetings did not take place, apart from Assembly meetings. So the Chamber is fully aware, and it's not the last word of this witness which is the final word for the Chamber. But we have to stop somewhere, because the risk is there that if we would continue with this line of questioning, that it would be one quarter of an hour to the left, another quarter of an hour to the right. I mean, the Chamber is aware of that. And that could perhaps continue for hours. So on the basis of the testimony given until now, the Chamber has decided that the -- this factual matter has been dealt with sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my -- my only submission on that is that what Your Honour sayings would, in principle, be more consonant, with respect, with a fair approach to this witness's evidence if the Trial Chamber's questions were not so clearly questions which were supportive of and consistent with what the Prosecution wished to get from this witness rather than what the Defence wished to get from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has noticed that you consider the questions of the witness to be supportive to the Prosecution and insupport [sic] of the Defence. The ruling is there. If you would have any further questions to the witness, we could ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. And if not ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, well, the only thing I did want to do, but if I need the witness back to do it, then the witness comes back to do it, is we would like the whole of the statements of this witness to be in evidence, not as his evidence, because he hasn't endorsed them all in that way, but we would wish the whole of those statements to go in and be available as part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could discuss this matter. Mr. Tieger, this has come into the mind of the Chamber as well, although we might have a slightly different approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I said statements. I beg your pardon. It was a slip of the tongue. Your Honour knows I mean the transcripts of the interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered whether we should admit them into evidence, which would make those transcripts exhibits. Because the relevant portions have been read to this witness. At the same time, the witness has read some B/C/S portions of the statement which are not in the transcript. He has done that during a break. So I'd like to hear from the parties whether it would be more appropriate to admit them into evidence or to mark them for identification so that at least the copies are there and that whomever at a later stage would like to see what the witness has read is able to do so. So should it be in evidence or should it just be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll just have a word, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the Defence would wish the documents to be in evidence, because we wish to be able to say: Yes, that's what -- that's what Mr. Radic did say on those occasions during the course of those interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's acceptable, Your Honour. If I could raise one minor point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will follow the preference of the Defence not objected by the Prosecution. If they are tendered, we'll admit them into evidence rather than to mark them for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would note with respect to a similar issue, there is a -- as I know counsel is aware, a similar reference to this issue in the Brdjanin transcript. I would like to have that -- I can either ask about it in redirect or have it just simply have it agreed upon for admission. It's just a few pages, roughly 22319, line 11 through 22321, line 10. But we're dealing with the matter in this fashion then it seems it would be more efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, in principle, what's sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander, as we say, Your Honour, as well. No, we couldn't possibly object to passages of the Brdjanin transcript going in in that way. Yes, that was the evidence given in the Brdjanin case. And if it turns out on examination that there might be more pages in due course which might be relevant, then we'll cross that bridge when we come to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The position of the parties is clear. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just like to note while -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, any further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The observation I was just going to make was that Ms. Cmeric has expressed quite a lot of unhappiness over the translation of those -- the transcripts of those interviews. I'm not entirely sure of the order of events as far as the translation is concerned, but we just want to have a look at that, Your Honour, and perhaps come back to it in due course. It's not something we can explore today anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. If there are any submissions to be made on incorrectness of translation of the statements, we can't deal with it at this point and at a later stage we'll have to find out whether it has had any influence on the testimony of this witness in this court. Mr. Tieger, any need for further questions to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you, Mr. Radic. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, I should like, please, to know a little more about this question that you were asked during your testimony, and I'm referring to what you said with respect to the interventions of deputies and their insistence upon the fact that you were not doing or not following the directives along the lines of having a presence, if I can put it that way, of the Croat and Muslim inhabitants, at least in the administration. Now, in this context, you were asked a specific question, and it was about realistic power, the realistic power that the deputies had. And you said, among other things, that: Yes, they did wield power, because they were the elected deputies, elected by the people. And you also added, and I'm quoting you in English: [In English] [Previous translation continues] "... and if they have a skilful leader like Krajisnik, then ..." [Interpretation] And that's where you stopped. Now, my first question is this: What were you going to add? What were you going to say in that context?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without a doubt, Mr. Krajisnik was very skilful. He was a very skilful leader and a very skilful president, who was well able to chair meetings and to have those meetings arrive at conclusions. Now, it's quite another matter how the deputies used that. Some of them would come with requests and demands that weren't discussed at all, nor were they made at National Assembly meetings. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] May I interrupt you there, Witness. I am interested more in knowing, within the scope of this subject, the interventions made by the deputies and their insistence upon the fact that there was a malfunctioning in Banja Luka in the extent to which you were not following the example set and the directives given obliging you to replace or get rid of or carry out a balancing policy, or expelling the non-Serb population, in view of their numbers, their existing numbers.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't receive any order to expel the non-Serb population. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] No, no. I wasn't speaking about orders. It seemed to me -- I seemed to understand you as saying that the deputies, five or six of them, at least, encouraged you to react differently, in the sense of getting rid of a certain number of non-Serb inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You also asked me whether they intervened to have Croats and Muslims dismissed from their jobs. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. And it is that subject that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to you, Your Honour, is the same answer that I gave here previously, that I did not allow, I did not permit people to be dismissed from their jobs. But not especially in the Municipal Assembly where they worked, not especially there. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that. But my interest lies elsewhere. We have the facts, and you have confirmed that the deputies intervened either to have you get rid of the non-Serb functionaries, officials, or -- and to expel a certain number of non-Serb inhabitants. So that's a question. Do you say yes or no? Was that the case or was it not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They couldn't say to me that I should expel them. What they said was that there were too many of them and that this should be solved and resolved in the same way it had been resolved in other municipalities. So you must know, Your Honour, that in the municipalities in Republika Srpska, the process had already been completed. And as it had indeed in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. But in your opinion, what was the relationship between those deputies and the Presidency of the Assembly, for example?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the type of relationship that always exists between the president of the Assembly and the deputies. What is concluded at the Assembly, the deputies were duty-bound to implement on the ground. But I saw on many occasions that what they had asked for was not the position taken by the People's Assembly itself. One of them asked for example that the vice-president of the Assembly be expelled from his office so that he could replace him. And when I said what are you doing he said he was interpreting the laws that were enacted at the Assembly and he was just a teacher. So there were cases and examples of that kind quite a lot but I was always opposed to that and I don't say that Mr. Krajisnik gave instructions to that effect at all. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] No. I'm not saying that. I should just like to go back to what you yourself said when you said that these deputies gained an importance, took on more importance through the fact that they had a skilful, as you yourself said, leader. Therefore, my question is quite simply this. It's a very simple question. I would like to understand what you have told us. So why, when it comes to deputies and their power, the power they yielded, did you add that they gained their importance or weight, that they gained more weight through the fact that they had a president who was indeed, as you said, skilful? So my question, quite simply, is this: The power that the president of the Assembly wielded, did it go beyond the powers of a president of a mere president of the Assembly? Or did he have the power that he exerted over his deputies and then this explains what you yourself said and quoted?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that they acted and behaved outside their competences and that Mr. Krajisnik was a very skilful president of the National Assembly who led them and solved problems with them. It does not mean that what they asked me to do that they ever heard that from him. And that proved to be so because what they asked me to do was something they could not have heard from Mr. Krajisnik, either at the National Assembly or elsewhere. So they came from those heights up above, took -- assumed this high-up position and tried to behave in that way. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And now this brings me to my last question, which has to do with what you said, and I'm quoting you [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... the unwritten rules." [Interpretation] You said that there were certain unwritten rules or directives which were applied in all the municipalities, in the sense of getting rid of the non-Serb inhabitants. Now, do you know something more about that, the source of those unwritten rules, where that came from?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those rules were not equal for all municipalities. It depended on who and how individual things were interpreted, things that -- decisions made by the government or brought up at assemblies. And one of them was this delocation of the population or the rationalisation of accommodation, as we referred to it. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Came from whom?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it came from those people who insisted upon the implementation of this and it reached the enterprises in some way. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [In English] Who are these people?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw the document myself, but it arrived at the enterprises and companies, and that's how they settled the question of their combatants, those who were factory employees. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And you didn't ask yourself where the documents emanated from, where they originated from? You didn't ask yourself that question, you didn't have information about the source of the documents?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because it was never brought up at the municipal meeting of Banja Luka, for example, Municipal Assembly meeting of Banja Luka. So I can't say if such a document existed, I can't say who gave such an instruction and that's what I said before. I said there were some very strange sources on the basis of which some people, for example, interpreted the fact that a music professor was at the source of information and that's why he should be dismissed from his job. So even if a document did exist, it had to have said that a music teacher was not an important -- importantly placed. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But a music teacher can also play a political role, can he not, and we have had testimony to the effect that there were certain refrains which represented an ethnicity, things that were said representing an ethnicity. So he wasn't an ordinary professor. For example, a professor of music can have political overtones. But let's move on. Anyway, with respect to what you said about the unwritten rules, what you're saying now is that you didn't have any information as to who these rules came from; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Although, as a rule, they would come to us, to the municipality, looking for protection. And we never adopted a document of that kind in the Assembly. We didn't get it from the National Assembly or from the government. We never received a document of that kind which would allow us to act that way in any particular case. So those are the sources on the basis of which things like that happened. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I have a few short questions for you. Would you please carefully listen to the question. First you testified about the knowledge of Mr. Sommaruga of, well, a large number of non-Serbs going through the territory of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then ... Yes. Yes. You said he was aware of that. Did he agree with these transports, in your view?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, no. Mr. Sommaruga. Because you told about his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Cornelio Sommaruga. Mr. Sommaruga came by helicopter. He flew over Banja Luka at a time when 250.000 Serbs from the Knin Krajina were passing through Banja Luka. And he was frightened of what he saw. Because the information he received was that in every second or third truck there were weapons. Now, had those people entered the city centre, they would have destroyed it. So we let them go, circumvent Banja Luka and pass around it. He saw President Koljevic's own [as interpreted]. They talked late into the night. Mr. Koljevic went to Pale and had a meeting with Mrs. Lucy Santer [phoen], and they wrote -- compiled a document about the voluntary departure of the non-Serb population, signed by Mrs. Lucy Santer and Mr. Koljevic, and I think that I gave a Mr. Conner that - Mrs. Conner - that document when she was in Banja Luka. Mrs. Korner. If you don't have it in your archives I shall be happy to send it to you both in English and in Serbian. So after that, as I say, that was the greatest exodus that took place, when the realisation of the treaty began to be implemented, the treaty on the departure of the population, where these people were taken off to the Croatian border. He was afraid that untoward incidents would take place when -- there was a clash with 250.000 armed Serbs who had been expelled from Croatia came to a head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd just allow me one second to reread your answer. It's still not entirely clear to me why the non-Serb population had to leave as a result of the arrival of 250.000 Serbs from the Knin Krajina. Because you put them in the same context.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not putting them in the same context, Your Honour. Mr. Cornelio Sommaruga put them in the same context because he was terribly afraid of the possible consequences of a clash breaking out between people left without their homes and saw that this place was inhabited by non-Serbs. So that was the reason. The reason was: Let's get rid of them for the time being until this convoy of 250.000 people goes through and then have the population return. And I can tell you that in Banja Luka, 95 per cent of the property that was not destroyed was returned to the Muslims and Croats. That is what is happening in Prijedor, and so on and so forth, elsewhere. So that was his idea because he was petrified, and I think he was right to have been petrified and terribly afraid of this happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now understand better the context. Did you ever visit the Omarska camp when there was -- when there were still detainees? I'm just asking you whether you did or not.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What caused you to visit Omarska camp? What was the reason why you went there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that the organisation of that visit, and I myself, well, yes, I did have reason to go and see it but the organisation of the visit was Mr. Brdjanin, because he wished to have a see whether anything could be done to get those people away from there. That was his initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you aware of a situation that existed that perhaps should change?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw what the situation was, I immediately asked the representative of the ICRC to go and register those people urgently. Because once their names are taken down and listed in the camp, then you put an end to all unfortunate incidences, anything evil happening. And then I asked him if we could find a way to get the people away altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was focusing on what you knew before you went to Omarska, because I do understand your last answer to be that when you saw what the situation was during your visit, what did you know or what did you hear or see about possible situations in Omarska before you went there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that immediately after the events, that information did pour into us. They even suggested from the Prijedor authorities that they would send these people to us to Banja Luka, for example. What would we do with all those people in Banja Luka in addition to all the refugees that we had from all over Bosnia-Herzegovina coming to us and from the Knin Krajina? So what I did then was I went to see for myself. I responded to the invitation and went to see for myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said that immediately after the events, that information did pour into us. Could you tell us what information. That's one. And then by which means that came to you.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The links between Prijedor and Banja Luka were not severed. People who had relatives in Omarska, for instance, came and said what was going on there. And it was through them that I learnt that the people were living in terrible conditions on the premises of an Omarska mine, others in Keraterm, which was a tile factory. They were completely inappropriate conditions. Nobody had prepared for that. They just put the people in these premises, the premises they had. But they had no proper conditions to accommodate those people. And when I saw Omarska, I had had enough. I'd seen enough. I came back and said what I said, what I told Mr. Manning [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You now told me what information came to you, and you mentioned as the source relatives from Omarska. And you said: "For instance, came to see you." Were there any other sources of information, apart from the relatives that came to you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that kind of information was not given out in the papers, in the form in which I saw things. Quite simply, the detainees, the prisoners in Omarska and in Keraterm were there, but I learnt the real truth of the matter from the Serbs, whose parents, for example, lived nearby, were near the Omarska mine and detention facility, for example, and of course, afterwards bench called us to have a look for ourselves and we saw it all. We didn't receive any other information, because not everybody had access to those sites, just the people that were allowed in, permitted to enter, asked to be allowed in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there any foreign media coverage that gave you some information?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, at that time, no, they could not. The foreign media could have access only once the people had been transferred to the military barracks at Manjaca. Then they could go up to them and talk to them. But otherwise, while they were down there, no, they couldn't. It was all blocked off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How were you aware that the foreign media could have access once the detainees were transferred to Manjaca? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they came to see me too. Because, as far as I was concerned, Manjaca, for us, the civilian authorities, was ex-territorial. It was a military facility, a military premises. And when they came back from there, I remember Jelinek, a lady journalist from Austria, a case in point, she came to see me and then we discussed that whole issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see the result of this press coverage in any way on television broadcasted? I mean, those journalist reports. Did you see them?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for journalist reports from that locality in Republika Srpska, no. They were not broadcast. They were broadcast in Austria, in Holland. There were some even in Norway. Broadcast in the countries from which those journalist had come to film it all. There were even -- there was even a crew from Japan, for example. But quite understandably, you couldn't have had Japanese reports and Norwegian reports and it was only after all that that I learnt from some journalist that they had filmed all this, of course with the presence of representatives of the ICRC and the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you satisfied with the conditions in which the detainees were in Manjaca, once transferred to there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: Whether I was satisfied or not is of a lesser importance. But I was dissatisfied, let me say, because there weren't the proper conditions there. Right up until the International Committee of the Red Cross arrived and organised health protection, they clothed the people and asked to have the proper standards, or at least the kind of standards that those barracks could provide. Otherwise, where they were, the conditions were very poor, very bad. But once again let me say they were better than they had been at Omarska and Keraterm, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you participate in any way to have the conditions in Manjaca improved? I do understand that it was a military facility, as you told me. Did you address the military or did you address anyone else to improve the situation?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the International Red Cross committee existed and that I did everything I could in my power to ensure that they had access, to ensure medical protection and care, and of course they had food and they had clothing and they had blankets and everything else that was necessary. And they sent it up there. Banja Luka at that time didn't have all this. They didn't have enough food for it to be able to send food out to that military facility. So, as I say, what we could do, we did. And of course, after that, there was organised transport from the civilian airport in Banja Luka from whence they were flown out all over Europe and got out of there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Communication with the ICRC, was that done on the municipal level or any other level?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a regional level where we were, because they covered a broader area. So they covered an area that was, for example, under Muslim and Croatian jurisdiction. They went there too, with their help and assistance, from Banja Luka. So that it was of a regional character, a broad regional character. And the very fact that the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, for example, came to Banja Luka frequently and visited Banja Luka and Sarajevo, speaks to the fact that this was indeed a regional centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The decision on whether or not to cooperate with or to lend assistance to the ICRC, was that a decision taken on the regional level or would that need any approval from other levels?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, when these matters are discussed, I wouldn't ask for any sort of an approval. But I must say that the vice-president of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, the late Nikola Koljevic, he was in charge for these matters. And I had his full support in this area. In addition to this, as vice-president, he was in charge within the Presidency for the humanitarian matters with the international community. Of course, I had his support and was able to have his approval, sometimes even before informing him of anything, he had already undertaken some actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Informing him about what?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of these events, about what I think needed to be undertaken. He never opposed me. Quite the contrary; I think that he encouraged Ms. Lucy Santer and others who were in charge of Bosnia-Herzegovina to do whatever was in their power. I must say that late Nikola Koljevic, he was a professor, a Shakespeareologist and humanitarian, and whatever is -- despite of what is being said about him, he was a human being in the true sense of the word. One could rely upon him and he was -- and he stayed in Banja Luka very often, because he hailed from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said he took action already before you informed him. Did you ever in your conversations or discussions or communication with him, did you ever experience that he was aware already of the situation you just described for Omarska and Keraterm as -- I think as terrible conditions and unsatisfactory conditions in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very fact of him intervening immediately speaks to the fact that he was informed, that he merely was looking for a way to solve the situation in a way that will be most favourable for the people. But he reacted, intervened immediately, and equally so, he stayed late with Mr. Cornelio Sommaruga at a meeting, until midnight. The very next morning, he was with Lucy Santer drafting the document, signing the agreement, and immediately they started providing for these 250.000 Serbs who were very narrow-minded, especially because of the fact that they had been expelled from an area they had lived for centuries, so they immediately started to try and remove them from the area. They had been expelled from Kordun, Banija, and Lika.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So is it a correct understanding of your testimony that you understood Mr. Koljevic's actions based on similar knowledge as you had about these conditions?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very fact that he reacted immediately shows that he must have known. He probably was well informed about the goings-on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These were my questions. Is there any need to put any further questions to the witness on the basis of issues raised by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. One issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. Further examination by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, Judge El Mahdi asked you a few questions about the power of the deputies and the relationship between their power and the skilfulness of their leader, in the words that you used in your interview. Now, this is also a matter that was raised and that you discussed during the course of your testimony in the Brdjanin case; is that correct? Just yes or no, sir.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. May I say -- yes, yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I could direct your attention to comments beginning on page 22134, line 13. You had been asked a question about a decree issued by Dr. Karadzic. You said: "That's something else so forget about what I said above about the decree law issued by Mr. Karadzic and we'll refer to the part which starts with we were a lower municipal level for them and that is how they behaved. Is that what you're asking me about now?" Question: "Exactly but I don't need you to read it all out, Mr. Radic. Everybody's read it. I'm just asking you if that's what you were saying in terms, in other words, if it was people at the level of deputies like Krajisnik, like Karadzic, and like Mr. Brdjanin, who were planning these matters which then were given as orders to the municipal levels." Answer: "What I wanted to say is quite clear in the text. I said that the deputies thought that they were more important than people at the municipal level and that is how they behaved. I said if they had such a masterful leader as Krajisnik, it resulted from all of this. I never mentioned Karadzic as someone who participated in this." That ends at page 22135, line 1. Understanding that masterful in that context very may well be more correctly translated as skilful, were those your comments, Mr. Radic, during the course of the Brdjanin case, with respect to this passage in the interview?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this expression here, masterful leader, I've said several times already that this term "leader," "vodja," in B/C/S, that the English term is the correct one. Because in B/C/S, the term vodja perhaps should be interpreted differently. I -- that is not what I had in mind. I've said a moment ago -- I apologise. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As such you may continue but let me first ask one thing to the parties. The question was whether this is the testimony of this witness in the Brdjanin case. I do understand that the portions of the Brdjanin testimony will be tendered into evidence anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I hadn't specifically identified that and we can dispense with the issue that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour we were asking ourselves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- one answer, but we didn't bother to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any questions, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. We -- Ms. Cmeric suggests, and actually even without being able to follow the B/C/S, it seems she must be right, that that answer the witness just gave at page 76, lines 3 to 7, it seems to be completely mangled, because first of all -- I don't think the witness could have said: "I said several times already this term leader" and then he gives a B/C/S word, that the English term is the correct one. He must be saying it wasn't the correct one. And then Ms. Cmeric tells me that the rest of the answer has got mangled up in some way as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we ask the witness -- You're not asked now any more whether this was your testimony in the Brdjanin case but you made some comments on the translation of the word "vodja." Could you please give them so that we can hear them. So you started that you were then interrupted and there was so the confusion anyhow. So could you please repeat or tell us what you wanted to tell us at that moment about the term vodja?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put it simply, I believe it quite sufficient to say "president of the parliament." Now, a leader, a ringleader, that is something that could be perceived in our language as in a pejorative manner, so not just as a person who is leading someone. So to say president of a National Assembly is quite enough. I've never said that he's a leader, vodja, in B/C/S. And there's another matter that I would like to address you, if -- with your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, to -- I now understand that you said you never used the word just pronounced, vodja, and that would have been the term you would have used if you would have referred to him as a leader. And you did not use that term.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Leader could be a party leader, whereas the president of the Assembly is the president of the Assembly. But there's another matter that I wanted to apply to you on. Do I have your leave? Throughout the documents here, two things have constantly been present. In those interviews with Ms. Korner. There were some interruptions with several dots there, where it said that Mr. Krajisnik was skilful. That was -- and then there are some dots following that. And implicitly one could perceive the "him" there as being a manipulator in that sense being skilful, whereas I just wanted to say that he was a skilful president of the National Assembly and he was skilful in running it. Now, what the implementation was like by others, that's something that I told you about. And that's why I also said -- I used the term "Deputate," meaning in that Soviet sense because they thought of themselves very highly, thought of themselves as being superior to the people they were representing. That's how they behaved. And that's why I called them Soviet "deputate."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you once again for clarifying these two issues, Mr. Radic. This conclude your testimony in this court. You've answered the questions of the parties and of the Bench. I would like to thank you very much for having done that and I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a few practical matters. The witness scheduled for tomorrow is a witness which testifies through a videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We have another witness scheduled for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We had another witness scheduled for today, Mr. Odobasic, but we weren't able to get to him. We anticipated the videolink would take precedence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I understood. Do you know how much time you would need approximately for - I haven't go the schedule in front of me - for the videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That videolink is only for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- I -- yes. Since the examination-in-chief, Mr. Stewart, took a little bit over two hours, could you give us an indication on how much time you would need for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd indicated to the Prosecution earlier this morning that I expected to complete cross-examination before the second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be three hours. And that is for two hours and 18 minutes in chief, is quite lengthy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm just indicating what I said to the Prosecution earlier this morning, Your Honour. But I can't actually remember offhand whether Mr. Biscevic's evidence was shortened by 89(F), which obviously affects the guidelines every time. But I was just trying to do my best there. And I'm aware of the guidelines, Your Honour, which we pretty consistently come well within on the Defence side anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would not contradict that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With appreciation, I do this. Because we have another few matters on our agenda as well, that is, the parties were invited to give their views on the -- I would say the overall schedule. Perhaps we could find time tomorrow for that as well. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure what Mr. Odobasic's schedule is. I know next week we have three days and we only have two witnesses. There's a possibility that if we could get Mr. Odobasic done tomorrow, we might have more time Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, to discuss additional issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Backgrounds that was one of the other -- one of the other procedural issues is whether or not the parties finally could agree on the schedule which would include a possibility for the investigators to visit The Hague and not to lose too much time in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had agreed with the Defence that we thought they could use Thursday and Friday for their meeting next week and that we would then only have witnesses Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but how many witnesses in view of the original schedule would we lose?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One would be pushed over to begin on the 8th of November. That was Mr. Cengic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Scheduled for how long approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Four and a half hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Four and a half hours. We'll consider that. Then another outstanding issue we still have is Exhibits 200 to 203.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's again my responsibility. I have sent an e-mail to Mr. Resch to try and obtain the information from him. I've advised Mr. Acquaviva of my awaiting that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you in one way or another speed that up --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so we could finally deal with these matters. Then one -- perhaps a bit more urgent matter is when can we receive the information asked at the beginning of this session? Because we have to take a decision. No. Let me just turn into private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. The Registry will be instructed that the latter part of the transcript will be made public and not remain confidential, as it is now. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.
